## 9. The findings ledger

`docs/pr_review_management.md` records the audit failure this replaces:
review feedback lived on three separate GitHub surfaces — inline
`pulls/N/comments`, issue-level `issues/N/comments`, and review summaries
`pulls/N/reviews` — and PRs were merged with comments nobody had read.  The
GraphQL `reviewThreads` `isResolved` / `isOutdated` pair was the only reliable
status signal; the REST `line` field lied.

Locally there is **one** surface.  Every finding lives on one line of the
`## Findings` section of the exact-head `COMMENT` review body, between
`<!-- findings:begin -->` and `<!-- findings:end -->`:

    - [ ] F1 (blocker) `MIPStarRE/Basic.lean:120` — adds a non-paper hypothesis

| Box | Meaning | Blocks merge |
|---|---|---|
| `[ ]` | unresolved | **yes** |
| `[x]` | resolved — a human or an agent addressed it and says so | no |
| `[-]` | outdated — the cited lines were rewritten since the reviewed SHA | no |

`[ ]` → `[x]` is a human judgement, or a claim by the fixer that a human is
expected to check; it is never automatic.  There is no automatic `[ ]` → `[-]`
pass: exactly one review is published per head SHA and the merge gate reads only
that one, so a finding written against an older SHA can no longer block and has
nothing to be outdated *out of*.  `[-]` stays available as a hand-written
disposition; a reviewer re-derives its findings from the new diff on every head.

**Merge gate.**  A PR whose current-head review carries any `[ ]` finding is
not mergeable.  The contract for `pr_merge.py` and for humans is exactly the
unchecked-finding regex of `issues-prs.md` §2, `^\s*[-*]\s*\[ \]`, applied to
the marker-bound review body for the head SHA; no match means the ledger is
clean, and the paired `local-review/summary` status must agree.  Anything else
must be resolved, outdated, or adjudicated by the operator under §12 (Round cap
and operator adjudication) — the operator is the adjudicating party; the owner
is consulted only for the escalations named in the standing briefing.  Owner
decision 2026-09-02 (EVOLUTION.md): this supersedes the GitHub-era "never merge
without consulting the user" rule of `docs/pr_review_management.md` for this
repository; the substantive review criteria are unchanged.

Findings do **not** survive across SHAs.  Gate 4 matches the marker
`<!-- mipstarre-review pr=N head=SHA -->` on that exact commit id, so a ledger
written at SHA *A* is invisible at SHA *B* — and a head carrying no review at
all is "not reviewed", never clean.  A finding that still applies is one the
next review re-derives from the new diff.

A second review of the **same** SHA replaces that SHA's ledger, including any
`[x]` a human had set.  `review.sh` copies the previous file into the run
directory as `<name>.superseded` and warns when it did so, but it does not
merge the two ledgers: a re-review is a new opinion about the same commit, and
silently carrying resolutions across it would let a resolved-then-reintroduced
finding disappear.  Resolve findings on the SHA you intend to keep.

## 10. `agent.sh` versus `autofix.sh`

`docs/pr_review_management.md` keeps a behavioural matrix for the `@claude` and
`@codex` responders — mentions fire only from comments and never from bodies;
`@codex` on an issue always forks a fresh PR from `main`, causing PR
proliferation; `@claude` on a PR pushes to the branch but failed outright on
branch names containing `]`, root-caused to `claude-code-action`'s branch-name
validation and fixed by adopting bracket-free naming
(`docs/pr_review_management.md:163`, `CONTRIBUTING.md:122-124`).

The local translation is:

| Parent | Local | Who starts it |
|---|---|---|
| `@claude` on a PR comment | `local/bin/agent.sh <pr-id> "instruction"` | a human, always |
| `@codex` on an issue | `local/bin/agent.sh <issue-id> "instruction"` | a human, always |
| auto-fix workflows | `local/bin/autofix.sh <pr-id> --mode ...` | CI/review chain or a human |

`agent.sh` is **never invoked by automation.**  `claude.yml:24-30` gated the
responder on `sender.type != 'Bot'` because a bot echoing `@claude` into a
comment would start a write-enabled, secret-bearing session; the local form is
that `review.sh` and `autofix.sh` export `MIPSTARRE_AUTOMATION=1` (and
`MIPSTARRE_AUTOFIX_ACTIVE=1`) around every agent they run, and `agent.sh`
refuses to start when either is set.  `agent.sh` also refuses while a fix lock
is held for its branch: two writers on one branch is the parallel-push
collision that `auto-fix.yml:253-256` serialised away.

The author_association gate has no local analogue and is dropped — the human
running the command *is* the authorisation.  The `]`-in-branch-name lesson
survives as a lint in all three scripts.

`agent.sh` may commit; it must not use the `[codex-auto-fix]` /
`[codex-review-fix]` prefixes, because a human-directed commit must be
reviewable and those prefixes make the reviewer skip.  The script warns if the
session used one anyway.

The auto-create-PR step of `claude.yml` becomes a printed instruction rather
than an action: when a session on an issue branch produces commits, `agent.sh`
tells the operator to open the PR with `local/bin/pr_open.py`, which pushes the
branch and owns the branch-name lint (`local/protocols/issues-prs.md`).

## 11. Operating it

    local/bin/review.sh 7                # review PR 0007 at its current head
    local/bin/review.sh 7 --dry-run      # build diff and prompts, dispatch nothing
    LOCAL_REVIEW_ENABLED=false local/bin/review.sh 7    # confirm the kill switch

Exit codes: `0` reviewed or intentionally skipped · `1` usage/environment ·
`3` gate blocked (CI not green for this head) · `4` no parseable verdict.
Code 3 publishes nothing at all — the missing green `local-review/summary` is
the block.  Only code 4 publishes a `failure` `local-review/summary`, and
neither publishes a review.

Artefacts:

| Path | Committed | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| the exact-head `COMMENT` review on the PR | on GitHub | combined verdict, ledger, prose |
| `local-review/summary` on the head SHA | on GitHub | the gate-readable verdict |
| `~/.cache/mipstarre-dev/reviews/pr<N>/<sha>/` | no | diff, prompts, raw agent output |
| `~/.cache/mipstarre-dev/locks/review-<pr>.lock` | no | the review lock |

Every codex invocation goes through `local/bin/dispatch.sh` when it exists, so
the session is named, captured to `results/telemetry/sessions/<name>.jsonl` and
summarised into `results/telemetry/sessions.jsonl`
(`local/protocols/sessions.md`).  Without the dispatcher, `review.sh` falls
back to a direct `codex exec` and says loudly that the session will not appear
in the registry — an untracked session is lost research data, so the fallback
is a degradation, not an alternative.  `dispatch.sh` enforces
`LOCAL_REVIEW_ENABLED` for reviewer-role sessions independently; the two checks
agreeing is intentional redundancy.

Missing pieces degrade with a message, never silently: missing CI statuses
block, no `worktree-setup.sh` warns about a cold build cache, no codex CLI is a
hard error.  A GitHub failure is fatal — a verdict that cannot be published is
not a verdict.

## 12. Deliberately not ported

Untouched-code or new-mechanism findings are "out of scope -> issue #N".

* **Provider matrix** (`CLAUDE_CODE_REVIEW_PROVIDERS` → per-provider jobs).
  One reviewer session; the cascade
  `CLAUDE_CODE_REVIEW_PROVIDERS > CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER > anthropic` becomes
  `MIPSTARRE_REVIEW_MODEL > MIPSTARRE_CODEX_MODEL > the dispatcher's default`.
* **Fork check** (`head_repository.full_name != repo` → skip).  Every PR here
  comes from a branch of this single repository.
* **Thread resolution via `mcp__github__resolve_review_thread`.**  Replaced by
  the ledger checkbox; the reviewer is told not to attempt it.
* **`allowed-tools` presets and `allowed-tools.json`.**  codex sandbox modes
  (`read-only` for review, `workspace-write` for fixes) carry the same intent
  with a coarser grain: read-only genuinely prevents writes, which the
  allow-list only approximated.
* **`id-token`/OAuth plumbing, `LionSR/agent-ci-actions`, plugin marketplaces.**
  Local codex configuration replaces them (`.codex/`, `local/protocols/sessions.md`).


## 12. Round cap and operator adjudication (2026-08-30)

A PR receives at most **four** full review rounds. From the fifth round on,
the operator may close the loop by adjudication instead of iteration:

1. every remaining finding is either fixed, or converted to a tracked issue;
   the operator posts an **ADJUDICATION comment** on the PR — a body starting
   with `ADJUDICATION`, carrying `head=<final_head>`, and listing the last
   round's findings with every box ticked and a one-line disposition each
   (`fixed in <commit>` / `deferred to issue #NNNN: <reason>` /
   `moot: <reason>`);
2. the comment is the record; nothing local is written;
3. the merge commit names the adjudication and the issues created;
4. `pr_merge.py --adjudicated` accepts it in place of a clean verdict, and
   only for the current head — a stale `head=` is a refusal.

Nothing is dropped silently: an adjudicated finding lives on as an issue.
This mirrors the parent's combined bot-fix iteration cap with a single
terminal review (pr-review.yml:69-72). See EVOLUTION.md for the trigger.

1	# Mathematical Language Guidelines
     2	
     3	MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
     4	the formalization with the paper and blueprint.
     5	
     6	This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
     7	naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
     8	`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.
     9	
    10	## Scope
    11	
    12	These guidelines apply to:
    13	
    14	- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
    15	- module docstrings;
    16	- declaration docstrings;
    17	- documentation-visible section comments;
    18	- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
    19	- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
    20	- issue titles and issue bodies;
    21	- PR titles and PR descriptions.
    22	
    23	## Source of Truth
    24	
    25	Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:
    26	
    27	1. `references/ldt-paper/`
    28	2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
    29	3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files
    30	
    31	When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
    32	example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
    33	projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.
    34	
    35	## Reference Notation And Terminology
    36	
    37	The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
    38	reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
    39	docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
    40	without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.
    41	
    42	When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
    43	location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
    44	first applicable location in the following order:
    45	
    46	1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
    47	   differs from the paper;
    48	2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
    49	   family of declarations in that file;
    50	3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
    51	   blueprint;
    52	4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
    53	   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.
    54	
    55	The explanation should say:
    56	
    57	- the notation or term used in the paper;
    58	- the Lean object or name which represents it;
    59	- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.
    86	
    87	### Concrete examples
    88	
    89	The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
    90	codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
    91	others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
    92	process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
    93	assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
    94	paper or blueprint would recognize.
    95	
    96	| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
    97	|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
    98	| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
    99	| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
   100	| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
   101	| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
   102	| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
   103	| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
   104	| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
   105	| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
   106	| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
   107	| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |
   108	
   109	An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
   110	phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
   111	In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.
   112	
   113	File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
   114	named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
   115	exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.
   116	
   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124	
   125	Procedure:
   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   129	   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   131	   explicit argument.
   132	2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   133	   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   134	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   135	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   136	   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
   137	3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   138	   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
   139	4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   140	   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   141	   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   142	   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   143	   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   144	   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
   145	5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   146	   blueprint location it supports.
   147	
   148	### Legacy identifier treatment
   149	
   150	If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
   151	describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
   152	identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
   153	in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.
   154	
   155	Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   156	public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
   157	shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
   158	blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.
   159	
   160	## Review Checklist
   161	
   162	Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
   163	documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.
   164	
   165	- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
   166	      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
   167	      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
   168	      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
   169	      implementation-phase labels)?
   170	- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
   171	      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
   172	      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
   173	      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
   174	      source does not use them that way?
   175	- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
   176	      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
   177	      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
   178	      that order of preference?
   179	- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
   180	      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
   181	      construction they support?
   182	- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
   183	      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
   184	      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
   185	- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
   186	      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
   187	      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
   188	      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
   189	- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
   190	      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
   191	      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
   192	      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.
   193	
   194	Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
   195	relevant audit before changing names or prose.

    11	
    12	This chapter and the two that follow contain the proof of the soundness
    13	theorem for the Pauli basis test, Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, stated in
    14	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. Starting from a strategy that succeeds in the
    15	game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ with high probability, the proof
    16	constructs a representation of the Pauli group on the players' Hilbert space
    17	in several stages. In Section~\ref{sec:commutation} the strategy measurements
    18	are used to define a set of observables that correspond to a subset of the
    19	Pauli $X$ and $Z$ observables, and these observables are shown to
    20	approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In
    21	Section~\ref{sec:expanding}, ancillary registers containing EPR states are
    22	adjoined to the players' state, and a new set of approximately commuting
    23	observables acting on the expanded state is defined.
    24	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} combines the approximately commuting
    25	observables into a strategy for the \emph{classical} low individual degree
    26	test and applies the soundness theorem of that test to construct a single
    27	projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of them.
    28	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} uses this simultaneous measurement to
    29	construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, shows that it is close
    30	to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduces
    31	Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}. Section~\ref{sec:qld-prelim} below collects
    32	preliminary definitions and lemmas used throughout the analysis.

    37	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree polynomial classes]
    38		\label{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
    39		\lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc}
    40		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.TotalDegreePoly}
    41		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.DegPoly, MIPStarRE.QPBT.evalCoefficient}
    42		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.DegPoly.padTo, MIPStarRE.QPBT.EvaluatesTo, MIPStarRE.QPBT.evalOpt}

    44		\uses{def:line, def:line-representative, def:polyfunc}
    45		Given integers $d, m \geq 0$ and a prime power $q$, denote by
    46		$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables over
    47		$\F_q$ with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When
    48		the field is clear from context we write $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}$, and when
    49		the number of variables is also clear from context, $\mathrm{ideg}_d$. We
    50		denote by $\deg_d$ the set of polynomials with \emph{total} degree at
    51		most $d$.
    52		% The line-restricted classes below are introduced only implicitly in the
    53		% source, in the statement of the lemma labelled lem:qld-comm-line-cons,
    54		% which reads them as polynomials "defined on the line". The coefficient
    55		% reading adopted here follows the answer format of the decision procedure
    56		% of the low individual degree game (source figure fig:ld-decider) and the
    57		% representative convention of def:polyfunc; see the remark following this
    58		% definition.
    59		For a line $\ell \subseteq \F_q^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:line}) presented
    60		by a base point $u_0$ and a direction $v$ --- for the lines arising as
    61		question contents, the pair read off the line's description, whose base
    62		point is the canonical representative of
    63		Definition~\ref{def:line-representative} --- and an integer $c \geq 0$,
    64		we write $\deg_c(\ell)$ for the set of univariate polynomials of degree
    65		at most $c$, each given by its list of $c+1$ coefficients and identified
    66		by its polynomial representative rather than by the function it induces,
    67		as in Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}; the argument $\ell$ records the
    68		line to which such an answer refers, through the parameterization
    69		$t \mapsto u_0 + tv$. The cases used below are $\deg_d(\ell)$ and
    70		$\deg_{md}(\ell)$; whenever $d \leq md$, extending coefficient lists by
    71		zeros gives the inclusion $\deg_d(\ell) \subseteq \deg_{md}(\ell)$. For
    72		$f \in \deg_c(\ell)$, $u \in \ell$, and $a \in \F_q$, we say that $f$
    73		\emph{evaluates to $a$ at $u$}, written $f(u) = a$, if $f(t) = a$ for
    74		every $t \in \F_q$ with $u = u_0 + tv$. When $v \neq 0$ this $t$ is
    75		unique, so every $f$ evaluates at every point of $\ell$; when $v = 0$,
    76		so that $\ell = \{u_0\}$, exactly those $f$ that induce a constant
    77		function on $\F_q$ evaluate at $u_0$, to their constant value. An
    78		operator indexed by $f(u)$ is understood to be the zero operator when
    79		$f$ does not evaluate at $u$, and for a family $\{N_f\}$ indexed by
    80		$f \in \deg_c(\ell)$ we write
    81		$N_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot)=a]} = \sum_{f \colon f(u) = a} N_f$; when
    82		$v = 0$ the classes indexed by $a \in \F_q$ form a sub-measurement
    83		rather than a partition of the outcomes. The \emph{completed} family of
    84		evaluation classes is the family indexed by $a \in \F_q \cup \{\bot\}$
    85		obtained by adjoining the additional class
    86		$N_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot)=\bot]} = \sum_{f} N_f$, the sum over those
    87		$f$ that do not evaluate at $u$; when $\{N_f\}$ is a POVM,
    88		respectively a projective measurement, the completed classes form one
    89		as well, and when $v \neq 0$ the class
    90		$N_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot)=\bot]}$ is the zero operator.
    91	\end{definition}

    93	\begin{remark}[Line answers as coefficient lists]
    94		\label{rem:deg-line-representatives}
    95		The source refers to the elements of $\deg_{md}(\ell)$ as polynomials
    96		``defined on the line $\ell$'', that is, as functions on the point set
    97		of $\ell$, while its decision procedure expects each line answer as a
    98		list of coefficients. The two readings differ. When $md \geq q$,
    99		distinct coefficient lists induce the same function $\F_q \to \F_q$;
   100		and when $\ell$ has direction $v = 0$ --- a case the question
   101		distributions produce with positive probability

   103		the singleton $\{u_0\}$, so a function on $\ell$ retains only a single
   104		field element of the answer. Definition~\ref{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
   105		therefore adopts the coefficient reading, under which the strategy's
   106		line measurements are indexed by exactly the answers of the prescribed

   132	\begin{definition}[Commuting and anticommuting tuples]
   133		\label{def:anticommuting-tuple}
   134		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.PauliTuple}
   135		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsAnticommuting, MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsCommuting}

   137		% The quantity gamma is introduced in the source at eq:gamma-value, inside
   138		% the completeness analysis of the Pauli basis test; the definition below
   139		% is self-contained and does not depend on that occurrence.
   140		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:subfield-trace}
   141		For a tuple
   142		$\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z) \in (\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$, let
   143		\[
   144			\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\big( (r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)) \cdot (r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)) \big)\,,
   145		\]
   146		where $r_W \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_W)$ is the scalar multiple of the
   147		vector $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_W) \in \F_q^{M}$, the middle $\cdot$ is the
   148		$\F_q$-inner product of two vectors in $\F_q^{M}$, and
   149		$\tr = \tr_{q \to 2}$. The tuple $\omega$ is called \emph{anticommuting}
   150		if $\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma(\omega) = 0$.
   151	\end{definition}

   154	generalized Pauli observables $\tau^X(r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X))$ and
   155	$\tau^Z(r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z))$ commute
   156	(see Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation});
   157	this is the source of the terminology.

   456	\begin{proof}
   457		\uses{thm:naimark, def:tensor-product-value, def:tensor-product-strategy}
   458		Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), applied with the
   459		families of all of the first player's measurements on register
   460		$\mathsf{A}$ and all of the second player's on register $\mathsf{B}$,
   461		yields an auxiliary space and a projective sub-measurement replacing
   462		each family on each register, together with a product auxiliary state,
   463		such that every correlation
   464		$\bra{\psi} M^{x}_a \ot M^{y}_b \ket{\psi}$ of $\mathcal{S}$ is
   465		reproduced on the extended state. Each auxiliary space embeds into a
   466		register of finitely many qubits; extend each dilated sub-measurement
   467		to the enlarged register by adding to one fixed outcome both the
   468		projector onto the orthogonal complement of the embedded subspace and
   469		the residual projector of the sub-measurement. The outcome operators
   470		remain mutually orthogonal projectors, now summing to the identity,
   471		and no correlation changes: the complement projector annihilates the
   472		extended state, which is supported in the embedded subspace, and so
   473		does each residual projector, because for each question pair the
   474		reproduced correlations sum to one --- the original families being
   475		POVMs (Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-strategy}) --- which forces
   476		the projector $\Id$ minus the sum of each dilated sub-measurement to
   477		have zero mass on the extended state. Finally, since the auxiliary
   478		state is a product state, a unitary acting on each player's ancilla
   479		qubits alone carries it to $\ket{0 \cdots 0} \ot \ket{0 \cdots 0}$;
   480		conjugating the projective measurements by the same unitaries
   481		preserves projectivity and all correlations. The success probability
   482		of a strategy is a linear combination of its correlations, weighted by
   483		the question distribution and the win predicate
   484		(Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value}), and is therefore

    64	Call a tuple $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) \in (\F_q^m)^2

    70	\begin{fact}
    71	\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
    72		The probability that a tuple $\omega= (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$ sampled uniformly at random from $(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$
    73		is anti-commuting is at least 
    74		\[
    75			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big (1 - \frac{md}{q} \Big )  \cdot \frac{1}{2} \geq \Big (1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}.
    76		\]
    77		The probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least $\Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.

    80		First, note that $\ind_m(u_\xpt) = 0$ if and only if $u_\xpt = 0$. If $u_\xpt=0$ then $\omega$ is commuting. Otherwise, if $u_\xpt \neq 0$, then observe that for all $r_\xpt, r_\zpt, u_\zpt$,
    81		\begin{align*}
    82			\tr( (r_\xpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot
    83	                \ind_m(u_\zpt))) &= \tr( r_\xpt r_\zpt (\ind_m(u_\xpt) \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt))) \\
    84									&= \tr( (r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt))\;,
    85		\end{align*}
    86		where $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$.

    88		If $r_\xpt = 0$, then $\omega$ is commuting. Condition on $r_\xpt \neq 0$.  Since $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}\neq 0$ has total degree at most $md$, by the Schwartz-Zippel lemma the probability that $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is zero over a uniformly random choice of $u_\zpt$ is at most $md/q$. Conditioned on $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt) \neq 0$, the product $(r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ when $r_\zpt$ is chosen uniformly at random.

    90		The probability that $u_\xpt \neq 0, r_\xpt \neq 0, g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt) \neq 0$ is at least $(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot (1 - md/q)$ since $u_\xpt, r_\xpt, u_\zpt$ are chosen independently.

    95	In this appendix we often use the ``$\approx_\delta$'' notation to specify closeness of general operators (not necessarily POVMs) that are indexed by questions but not answers: given sets of operators $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ indexed by questions $x \in \cal{X}$, we write $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ to denote \[
    96		\E_{x \sim \mu} \bra{\psi} (A^x - B^x)^\dagger (A^x - B^x)
    97	        \ket{\psi}\,\leq\, O(\delta)
    98	      \]
    99	where $\mu$ is a question distribution and $\ket{\psi}$ is a state that has been fixed by context. This will be useful for expressing closeness of observables, for example. The following two lemmas relate the closeness between sets of operators and weighted sums of those operators. 
   100	\begin{lemma}
   101	\label{lem:avg-closeness}
   102	Let $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be operators indexed by some finite set $\mathcal{X}$, and let $\mu$ be a probability distribution over $\mathcal{X}$. Let $\{\alpha_x \}$ be a set of complex numbers such that $|\alpha_x| \leq 1$. Then if $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ on average over $x$ drawn from $\mu$, then $A \approx_\delta B$, where $A = \E_x \alpha_x A^x$ and $B= \E_x \alpha_x B^x$.
   103	\end{lemma}
   104	\begin{proof}
   105	Expand
   106	\begin{align*}
   107		\Big\| \E_x \alpha_x \big ( A^x - B^x \big) \ket{\psi} \Big\|^2 &\leq \Big( \E_x \norm{ (A^x -B^x) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   108		&\leq \E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   109		&\leq \delta\;.
   110	\end{align*}
   111	The first inequality is the triangle inequality and the second inequality is Jensen's inequality. 
   112	\end{proof}

   114	\begin{lemma}
   115	\label{lem:povm-to-obs}
   116	Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set. Let $\{A^x_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ and $\{B^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be POVMs and let $\{ \alpha_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a collection of complex numbers on the unit circle. Let $A^x = \sum_a \alpha_a A^x_a$ and $B^x = \sum_a  \alpha_a B^x_a$. Then 
   117	\[
   118		A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a \quad \text{implies} \quad A^x \approx_{\delta'} B^x
   119	\]
   120	for $\delta' = |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta$.
   121	\end{lemma}
   122	\begin{proof}
   123	Expand
   124		\begin{align*}
   125			\E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \Big\|\sum_a \alpha_a (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}\Big\|^2 \\
   126			&\leq \E_x \Big( \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   127			&\leq \E_x |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   128			&\leq |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta\;.
   129		\end{align*}
   130	The first inequality follows from the triangle inequality, the second inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz, and the last inequality follows from the assumption that $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$. 
   131	\end{proof}

   426	$M$ denotes the measurement operators of both players; which player is
   427	meant is indicated by the register on which the operator acts (for
   428	example, $M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \Id_{\mathsf{B}}$ indicates that

   432	The analysis requires the measurements of $\mathcal{S}$ to be projective;
   433	the following lemma shows that this may be assumed without loss of

   435	
   436	\begin{lemma}[Reduction to a projective strategy]
   437		\label{lem:projective-strategy-setup}
   438		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_projective_padded_strategy}
   439		\leanok
   440		\uses{def:admissible, def:pauli-question-distribution, def:pauli-win-predicate, def:tensor-product-strategy, def:tensor-product-value, def:projective-strategy-general}
   441		Let $(q,m,d)$ be an admissible parameter tuple
   442		(Definition~\ref{def:admissible}) and let
   443		$\mathcal{S} = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ be a strategy for the game
   444		$\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a
   445		bipartite state on registers $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$. Then there
   446		exists a projective strategy
   447		(Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy-general}) for
   448		$\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ whose success probability
   449		equals that of $\mathcal{S}$ and whose state is the extension
   450		\[
   451			(\ket{\psi} \ot \ket{0\cdots 0} \ot \ket{0\cdots 0})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}}
   452		\]
   453		of $\ket{\psi}$ by finitely many ancilla qubits initialized in the
   454		state $\ket{0}$, adjoined to each of the two registers.
   455	\end{lemma}
   456	\begin{proof}
   457		\uses{thm:naimark, def:tensor-product-value, def:tensor-product-strategy}
   458		Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), applied with the
   459		families of all of the first player's measurements on register
   460		$\mathsf{A}$ and all of the second player's on register $\mathsf{B}$,
   461		yields an auxiliary space and a projective sub-measurement replacing
   462		each family on each register, together with a product auxiliary state,
   463		such that every correlation
   464		$\bra{\psi} M^{x}_a \ot M^{y}_b \ket{\psi}$ of $\mathcal{S}$ is
   465		reproduced on the extended state. Each auxiliary space embeds into a
   466		register of finitely many qubits; extend each dilated sub-measurement
   467		to the enlarged register by adding to one fixed outcome both the
   468		projector onto the orthogonal complement of the embedded subspace and
   469		the residual projector of the sub-measurement. The outcome operators
   470		remain mutually orthogonal projectors, now summing to the identity,
   471		and no correlation changes: the complement projector annihilates the
   472		extended state, which is supported in the embedded subspace, and so
   473		does each residual projector, because for each question pair the
   474		reproduced correlations sum to one --- the original families being
   475		POVMs (Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-strategy}) --- which forces
   476		the projector $\Id$ minus the sum of each dilated sub-measurement to
   477		have zero mass on the extended state. Finally, since the auxiliary
   478		state is a product state, a unitary acting on each player's ancilla
   479		qubits alone carries it to $\ket{0 \cdots 0} \ot \ket{0 \cdots 0}$;
   480		conjugating the projective measurements by the same unitaries
   481		preserves projectivity and all correlations. The success probability
   482		of a strategy is a linear combination of its correlations, weighted by
   483		the question distribution and the win predicate
   484		(Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value}), and is therefore
   485		unchanged.
   486	\end{proof}

    29	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]

   275	      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   276	        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pauli W))
   277	  let basisEdges :=
   278	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   279	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pairW W)) ∪
   280	      ({Sym2.mk (.point .X) (.ms (.var ⟨0, by decide⟩)),
   281	        Sym2.mk (.point .Z) (.ms (.var ⟨4, by decide⟩))} : Finset (Sym2 PauliType))
   282	  let pairEdges :=
   283	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   284	      Sym2.mk (.pairW W) .pair)
   285	  let msEdges' :=
   286	    (Finset.univ : Finset (MsType × MsType)).filter (fun xy =>
   287	      Sym2.mk xy.1 xy.2 ∈ msEdges) |>.image (fun xy =>
   288	        Sym2.mk (.ms xy.1) (.ms xy.2))
   289	  loops ∪ lineEdges ∪ basisEdges ∪ pairEdges ∪ msEdges'
   290	
   291	/-- A Pauli question is a type together with a full ambient coefficient vector
   292	(`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper
   293	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
   294	-/
   295	abbrev PauliQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) := PauliType × PauliSpace P
   296	
   297	/-- The Pauli question carrying no additional coefficient data, as in
   298	`def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:356-392`, paper origin
   299	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1006-1008`.
   300	Its ambient coefficient vector is zero. -/
   301	def pauliQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind) : PauliQuestion P :=
   302	  (.pauli W, 0)
   303	
   304	/-- The ordered-edge subtype used by the Pauli question sampler.  This is
   305	the finite carrier underlying `graphDistribution pauliEdges`; it is Lean-only
   306	infrastructure for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
   307	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   308	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   309	-/
   310	abbrev PauliEdge :=
   311	  {e : PauliType × PauliType // Sym2.mk e.1 e.2 ∈ pauliEdges}
   312	
   313	/-- The Pauli graph has a loop, so its ordered-edge subtype is nonempty.  This
   314	is a finite-carrier fact used only to instantiate the uniform source sampler
   315	for `def:pauli-question-distribution`; the graph itself is the source-facing
   316	object `pauliEdges` above (same blueprint and paper references).
   317	-/
   318	theorem pauliEdge_nonempty : Nonempty PauliEdge := by
   319	  refine ⟨⟨(.point .X, .point .X), ?_⟩⟩
   320	  simp [pauliEdges]
   321	
   322	/-- The Pauli question distribution from `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   323	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   324	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1070-1120`.
   325	-/
   326	noncomputable def pauliQuestionDistribution (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   327	    Distribution (PauliQuestion P × PauliQuestion P) :=
   328	  by
   329	    classical
   330	    letI : Nonempty PauliEdge := pauliEdge_nonempty
   331	    exact
   332	      Distribution.map
   333	        (uniformDistribution (PauliEdge × PauliSpace P))
   334	        (fun s =>
   335	          ((s.1.1.1, pauliCL P s.1.1.1 s.2),
   336	            (s.1.1.2, pauliCL P s.1.1.2 s.2)))
   337	
   338	/-- The finite answer alphabet for the Pauli basis test.  Its constructors are
   339	the seven answer forms in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint lines 331-367,
   340	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   341	-/
   342	inductive PauliAnswer (P : AdmissibleParams) where
   343	  | value (a : PauliScalar P)
   344	  | alinePoly (a : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   345	  | dlinePoly (a : Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   346	  | pairBits (a : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2)
   347	  | bit (a : ZMod 2)
   348	  | msTriple (a : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
   349	  | pauliOutcome (a : PauliRegister P)
   350	  deriving DecidableEq
   351	
   352	/-- A formalization-only total relabeling from the global Pauli-test answer
   353	alphabet to a Pauli register. It folds wrong-form answers into zero so that a
   354	Pauli question yields a complete `PauliRegister`-indexed measurement. -/
   355	def pauliAnswerOrZero {P : AdmissibleParams} : PauliAnswer P → PauliRegister P
   356	  | .pauliOutcome u => u
   357	  | _ => 0
   358	
   359	/-- A finite sum code used only to construct the `Fintype` instance for the
   360	answer alphabet in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   361	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   362	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   363	-/
   364	abbrev PauliAnswerCode (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   365	  PauliScalar P ⊕
   366	    ((Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   367	      ((Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   368	        ((ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) ⊕
   369	          (ZMod 2 ⊕ ((Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ PauliRegister P)))))
   370	
   371	/-- The constructor-preserving finite-code equivalence for `PauliAnswer`.
   372	Lean-only infrastructure for `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   373	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   374	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   375	-/
   376	noncomputable def pauliAnswerEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   377	    PauliAnswer P ≃ PauliAnswerCode P where
   378	  toFun
   379	    | .value a => .inl a
   380	    | .alinePoly a => .inr (.inl a)
   381	    | .dlinePoly a => .inr (.inr (.inl a))
   382	    | .pairBits a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))
   383	    | .bit a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))
   384	    | .msTriple a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))))
   385	    | .pauliOutcome a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a)))))
   386	  invFun
   387	    | .inl a => .value a
   388	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePoly a
   389	    | .inr (.inr (.inl a)) => .dlinePoly a
   390	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))) => .pairBits a
   391	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))) => .bit a
   392	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))) => .msTriple a
   393	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a))))) => .pauliOutcome a
   394	  left_inv := by
   395	    intro x
   396	    cases x <;> rfl
   397	  right_inv := by
   398	    intro x
   399	    cases x with
   400	    | inl a => rfl
   401	    | inr x =>
   402	        cases x with
   403	        | inl a => rfl
   404	        | inr x =>
   405	            cases x with
   406	            | inl a => rfl
   407	            | inr x =>
   408	                cases x with
   409	                | inl a => rfl
   410	                | inr x =>
   411	                    cases x with
   412	                    | inl a => rfl
   413	                    | inr x =>
   414	                        cases x with
   415	                        | inl a => rfl
   416	                        | inr a => rfl
   417	
   418	noncomputable instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Fintype (PauliAnswer P) :=
   419	  Fintype.ofEquiv (PauliAnswerCode P) (pauliAnswerEquiv P).symm
   420	
   421	instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Inhabited (PauliAnswer P) :=
   422	  ⟨.bit 0⟩
   423	
   424	/-- The phase bit `γ(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)` from `eq:gamma-value`.  It uses the
   425	fixed trace selected by `P.model`, as required by the paper's fixed
   426	self-dual-normal representation.  Blueprint
   427	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   428	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   429	-/
   430	noncomputable def gammaValue (P : AdmissibleParams)
   431	    (uX uZ : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   432	    (rX rZ : PauliScalar P) : ZMod 2 :=
   433	  fixedBinTrace P.model
   434	    (dotProduct (rX • indicatorVec uX) (rZ • indicatorVec uZ))
   435	
   436	/-- The commutation bit attached to a full Pauli ambient question, from
   437	`eq:gamma-value` in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   438	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   439	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   440	-/
   441	noncomputable def pauliPairGamma (P : AdmissibleParams) (z : PauliSpace P) : ZMod 2 :=
   442	  gammaValue P (pauliXBlock z) (pauliZBlock z)
   443	    (pauliRXBlock z) (pauliRZBlock z)
   444	
   445	/-- The answer constructor prescribed by each Pauli question type; this is the
   446	well-formedness part of `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   447	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   448	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   449	-/
   450	def validPauliAnswer {P : AdmissibleParams} (t : PauliType) (a : PauliAnswer P) : Bool :=
   451	  match t, a with
   452	  | .point _, .value _ => true
   453	  | .aline _, .alinePoly _ => true
   454	  | .dline _, .dlinePoly _ => true
   455	  | .pauli _, .pauliOutcome _ => true
   456	  | .pairW _, .bit _ => true
   457	  | .pair, .pairBits _ => true
   458	  | .ms (.constraint _), .msTriple _ => true
   459	  | .ms (.var _), .bit _ => true
   460	  | _, _ => false
   461	
   462	/-- The axis-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   463	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   464	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   465	-/
   466	def pauliAlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   467	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   468	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   469	  -- The universal form preserves the source's zero-direction convention.
   470	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   471	    pauliPointBlock W point =
   472	        pauliPointBlock W line + t • coordinateDirection
   473	          (chiIndex P.toLdParams (pauliScalarBlock line)) →
   474	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   475

     6	/-!
     7	# The Pauli basis test
     8	
     9	This file supplies the finite question and answer alphabets, the typed
    10	conditionally-linear question sampler, and the Boolean win predicate for the
    11	Pauli basis test.  The quantitative soundness theorem is isolated in
    12	`Soundness.lean`.
    13	
    14	## References
    15	
    16	The source-facing nodes are `def:admissible`, `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
    17	and `def:pauli-win-predicate` in
    18	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-367`; their paper origin is
    19	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:908-1225`.
    20	-/
    21	
    22	open scoped BigOperators
    23	
    24	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    25	
    26	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    27	
    28	noncomputable section
    29	
    30	/-- The numerical admissible Pauli-test parameter package.  Its scalar carrier
    31	uses the once-and-for-all model `fixedFieldModel q hq`, so the paper's fixed
    32	self-dual-normal identification is not quantified in the test statement.  This
    33	is `def:admissible` in
    34	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
    35	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    36	-/
    37	structure AdmissibleParams where
    38	  q : ℕ
    39	  m : ℕ
    40	  d : ℕ
    41	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    42	  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
    43	  hdvd : m ∣ q
    44	
    45	/-- The positivity of the ambient dimension is a proof obligation implicit in
    46	the admissibility convention `def:admissible`, blueprint
    47	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
    48	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    49	-/
    50	theorem AdmissibleParams.one_le_m (P : AdmissibleParams) : 1 ≤ P.m := by
    51	  sorry
    52	
    53	/-- The fixed model accessor for an admissible parameter package.  It is a
    54	compatibility view of the global `fixedFieldModel` selector, not an independently
    55	quantified field representation.  Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`; paper
    56	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    57	-/
    58	noncomputable def AdmissibleParams.model (P : AdmissibleParams) : FixedFieldModel P.q :=
    59	  fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq
    60	
    61	/-- The low-degree parameter view of an admissible Pauli-test package.  This is
    62	a Lean-only bridge supporting the statement closure; it is not an additional
    63	hypothesis of `thm:pauli`.  Blueprint
    64	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    65	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    66	-/
    67	def AdmissibleParams.toLdParams (P : AdmissibleParams) : LdParams where
    68	  q := P.q
    69	  m := P.m
    70	  d := P.d
    71	  k := 1
    72	  hm := P.one_le_m
    73	  hd := P.hd
    74	  hk := by decide
    75	  hq := P.hq

     2	
     3	/-! # Polynomial error predicates
     4	
     5	Shared quantitative predicates for the polynomial-error bounds in QPBT
     6	chapters 12, 14, and 15.
     7	
     8	## References
     9	
    10	These are formalization-only auxiliaries for polynomially small QPBT error
    11	functions. The one-parameter form includes the explicit square-root witnesses
    12	in paper chapter 14; the two-parameter form is used by `lem:pasting` in paper
    13	chapter 6.
    14	-/
    15	
    16	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    17	
    18	/-- A nonnegative one-parameter error function bounded by a positive real power.
    19	
    20	**Local fix:** The prefactor and exponent are quantified separately. Paper
    21	chapter 14 explicitly obtains `sqrt ε` at
    22	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:508-520,649-676`, which the coupled
    23	constant in the shorthand at `04_preliminaries.tex:26-29` cannot bound on all
    24	positive inputs. The correction is documented in
    25	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_polynomial-error-square-root.tex` and tracked by issue
    26	#16. -/
    27	def IsPolyErr (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
    28	  ∃ C r : ℝ, 1 ≤ C ∧ 0 < r ∧ ∀ x, 0 ≤ x →
    29	    0 ≤ f x ∧ f x ≤ C * Real.rpow x r
    30	
    31	/-- The two-parameter polynomial bound used by `lem:pasting`: on positive
    32	arguments, one universal positive constant is both the prefactor and exponent.
    33	This is the convention of `04_preliminaries.tex:26-29`, applied at
    34	`06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:518-524`; blueprint
    35	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:442-469`. -/
    36	def IsPolyErr₂ (f : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
    37	  ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ x y, 0 < x → 0 < y →
    38	    0 ≤ f x y ∧ f x y ≤ C * Real.rpow (x * y) C
    39	
    40	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     5	/-!

     7	
     8	This file fixes a projective, possibly heterogeneous strategy for the Pauli
     9	basis test and extracts the typed measurement families used in the analysis.
    10	Malformed answers are folded into a fixed valid answer, so the extracted
    11	families remain complete measurements. Their original wrong-form mass is kept
    12	separately and bounded by named proof obligations. `Option` is used only for
    13	the completed line-evaluation classes.
    14	
    15	## References
    16	
    17	The ambient strategy convention and the observable `W^r(u)` are in
    18	`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:160-190`,
    19	corresponding to `def:strategy-observables` in
    20	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:480-503`. The typed question
    21	and answer forms come from `def:pauli-question-distribution` and
    22	`def:pauli-win-predicate`, paper
    23	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1225`
    24	and blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:310-392`.
    25	-/
    26	
    27	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    28	
    29	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    30	
    31	open MIPStarRE.LDT MIPStarRE.Quantum
    32	
    33	noncomputable section
    34	
    35	/-- The two local registers of a heterogeneous bipartite strategy. This is
    36	formalization-only indexing for the player-dependent notation at paper
    37	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:160-190`. -/
    38	inductive PlayerSide where
    39	  | alice
    40	  | bob
    41	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    42	
    43	/-- A projective strategy satisfying the winning premise used throughout
    44	Section `sec:commutation`. The structure retains the distinct player spaces and
    45	measurement families of `Strategy`. Paper
    46	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:160-172`; blueprint
    47	`ch14_qpbt_observables.tex:385-475`. -/
    48	structure ProjectiveSetting (P : AdmissibleParams) (ε : ℝ) where
    49	  toStrategy : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P)
    50	  isProjective : toStrategy.IsProjective
    51	  win : 1 - ε ≤ toStrategy.value
    52	
    53	namespace ProjectiveSetting
    54	
    55	variable {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε : ℝ}
    56	
    57	/-- The local Hilbert-space index type on a specified player side. This is the
    58	dependent carrier behind the side-qualified operators at paper
    59	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:174-190`. -/
    60	def LocalSpace (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) : PlayerSide → Type
    61	  | .alice => S.toStrategy.ιA
    62	  | .bob => S.toStrategy.ιB
    63	
    64	instance localSpaceFintype (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide) :
    65	    Fintype (S.LocalSpace side) := by
    66	  cases side <;> simp only [LocalSpace] <;> infer_instance
    67	
    68	instance localSpaceDecidableEq (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide) :
    69	    DecidableEq (S.LocalSpace side) := by
    70	  cases side <;> simp only [LocalSpace] <;> infer_instance
    71	
    72	/-- Select the strategy measurement before outcome postprocessing on one
    73	player side. This is the heterogeneous interpretation of the shared symbol `M` at
    74	paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:160-184`. -/
    75	def rawMeasurement (S : ProjectiveSetting P ε) (side : PlayerSide)
    76	    (question : PauliQuestion P) :
    77	    Measurement (PauliAnswer P) (S.LocalSpace side) := by
    78	  cases side with
    79	  | alice => exact S.toStrategy.A question
    80	  | bob => exact S.toStrategy.B question
    81	
    82	/-- Embed a point into the full Pauli question space in basis `W`. This is the
    83	point-question content from `def:pauli-question-distribution`, paper
    84	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:997-1008`, blueprint
    85	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:310-354`. -/
    86	def contentOfPoint (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
    87	    (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) : PauliSpace P :=
    88	  embedLd P W fun i =>
    89	    match i with
    90	    | .inl (.inl j) => u j
    91	    | .inl (.inr _) => 0
    92	    | .inr _ => 0
    93	
    94	/-- Embed a canonical line description into the full Pauli question space.
    95	Axis lines clear the direction block, whereas diagonal lines retain their
    96	canonical projected direction. Paper
    97	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:997-1008`; blueprint
    98	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:310-354` and `rem:deg-line-representatives`. -/
    99	def contentOfLine (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   100	    (line : LineDesc P.toLdParams) : PauliSpace P :=
   101	  embedLd P W fun i =>
   102	    match i with
   103	    | .inl (.inl j) => line.base j
   104	    | .inl (.inr _) => line.seed
   105	    | .inr j =>
   106	        match line with
   107	        | .axis _ _ _ => 0
   108	        | .diagonal _ _ direction _ _ => direction j
   109	
   110	/-- Fill the point, scalar, and phase blocks shared by Pair, Pair/W, and Magic
   111	Square questions. This is the type-4 content of
   112	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, paper
   113	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1030-1120`, blueprint
   114	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:310-354`. -/
   115	def contentOfTuple (P : AdmissibleParams)
   116	    (uX uZ : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) (rX rZ : PauliScalar P) : PauliSpace P :=
   117	  fun i =>
   118	    match i with
   119	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) => uX j
   120	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) => uZ j
   121	    | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => 0
   122	    | .inl (.inl (.inr _)) => 0
   123	    | .inl (.inr _) => rX
   124	    | .inr _ => rZ
   125	
   126	/-- The typed point question in basis `W`, from the strategy notation at paper
   127	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:174-190` and
   128	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:310-354`. -/
   129	def pointQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   130	    (u : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) : PauliQuestion P :=
   131	  (.point W, contentOfPoint P W u)
   132	
   133	/-- The typed axis or diagonal line question represented by a canonical
   134	`LineDesc`. Paper `14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:174-184`; blueprint
   135	`def:strategy-observables` and `rem:deg-line-representatives`. -/
   136	def lineQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   137	    (line : LineDesc P.toLdParams) : PauliQuestion P :=
   138	  match line.kind with
   139	  | .axis => (.aline W, contentOfLine P W line)
   140	  | .diagonal => (.dline W, contentOfLine P W line)

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
